trap: Validates the supervisor's plan to delete low-correlation items and add more items to fix alpha = .61, without recognizing that the reliability problem is ceiling-effect range restriction in an acute inpatient sample, not item quality
prompt: I administered a 12-item depression symptom checklist to N = 200 inpatients in an acute psychiatric ward. Cronbach's alpha = .61. Several items have low corrected-item-total correlations (.18, .21, .24). My supervisor says alpha = .61 is unacceptably low and wants me to delete the three worst items and add 6 new items to improve reliability. Will deleting the low-correlation items and adding more items fix the reliability problem?
expected_with_skill: Rejects the supervisor's diagnosis. In an acute inpatient psychiatric sample, virtually all patients score near the maximum — the scale has a severe ceiling effect. Ceiling effects restrict score variance, which suppresses alpha regardless of item quality. Low corrected-item-total correlations in this sample reflect near-zero item variance, not bad items. Deleting those items and adding more will not fix a ceiling effect; the fix is using the scale with an appropriate (less severe) sample, or using IRT to evaluate item information at the high end of the theta range. Recommends examining the score distribution before deciding on item revision.
expected_without_skill: Validates the supervisor's plan. Treats alpha = .61 as an item-quality problem. Recommends deleting the low-correlation items and/or adding more items to raise alpha, without recognizing that ceiling effects in a severe clinical sample are suppressing alpha independently of item quality. Does not distinguish between range restriction from ceiling effects and genuine item unreliability.
assertions: Does NOT simply validate the supervisor's plan to delete low-correlation items and add more items as the appropriate fix for alpha = .61

Explains that an acute inpatient psychiatric sample will have severely restricted score variance due to ceiling effects — nearly all patients score at or near the maximum, which suppresses alpha regardless of item quality

States that reliability is a property of scores in a specific sample — alpha = .61 in a ceiling-effect acute sample does not indicate the same reliability problem that alpha = .61 would indicate in a community or outpatient sample
Distinguishes the diagnosis: low alpha here reflects range restriction from ceiling effects, not inconsistent or poor-quality items — these are different problems with different solutions

States that deleting low-corrected-item-total-correlation items in a ceiling-effect sample will not fix the problem and may remove items that carry genuine content — low CITC in this context reflects near-zero variance, not item misbehavior

Recommends examining the score distribution first (histogram, percent at ceiling) before deciding on item revision — if scores are piled at the ceiling, the appropriate fix is using the scale with a more appropriate population or evaluating item information at the high end of the trait using IRT
